faqs.question: When is Propose Day 2027?
faqs.answer: Monday 8 February 2027. It is the second day of Valentine week, after Rose Day on Sunday 7 February, and the week closes with Valentine's Day on Sunday 14 February.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a Propose Day wish and a Propose Day quote?
faqs.answer: A wish is addressed to one named person and sent; a quote is a general line written by someone else and copied. Putting a colleague's name on a quote is what turns a greeting into an accidental confession.

faqs.question: Can I send Propose Day wishes to a friend?
faqs.answer: Yes, and most people do. Keep it explicitly plural or explicitly platonic, send it mid-morning rather than late at night, and use plain text rather than a built page.

faqs.question: Is it odd to send Propose Day wishes to a work group?
faqs.answer: Not if the wording makes clear nobody is proposing to anybody. Group wishes belong in the 10 am to noon window, where they read as a greeting rather than as something aimed at one person.

faqs.question: What time should I send a Propose Day message on a working Monday?
faqs.answer: Before 8 am for warmth with no obligation, 10 am to noon for friends and groups, 1 pm to 2 pm if you actually want a reply, and after 10 pm only for the one person you mean it about.

faqs.question: My Propose Day message shows as read but there is no reply. What does that mean?
faqs.answer: Usually nothing about the relationship. A 2020 study of 213 college students in Japan found negative emotions arrive faster while waiting on a message already marked read than on an unread one, so the blue ticks are doing the damage, not the delay.

faqs.question: Should I propose over text on Propose Day?
faqs.answer: No. Send a notice that you are going to ask, then ask in person. A message is a good way to stop someone being ambushed and a poor way to ask the question itself.

faqs.question: Can I send Propose Day wishes to my wife or husband?
faqs.answer: Yes — a wish expects no answer, so a spouse is a normal recipient. The 6 pm to 8 pm window suits it, because a message then gets read rather than glanced at.

faqs.question: Which SubhSandesh page should I use for a Propose Day message?
faqs.answer: Use /proposal only if you are genuinely asking. For a partner you already have, /love-gf fits better; for a friend or sibling, neither fits and plain text is correct.

faqs.question: How long before the evening should I start building a page?
faqs.answer: Start by mid-afternoon. The median gap from a page's first save to its last edit is 2.4 hours, sampled on /apology-dashboard at n=1,348 and not on any proposal page, so an 8 pm send needs a 5 pm start.

faqs.question: Is a Propose Day wish the same thing as shayari?
faqs.answer: No. Shayari is a verse form with its own metre and conventions; a wish is prose, addressed to one person, and expects nothing back.

faqs.question: Should I post my Propose Day wish publicly or send it privately?
faqs.answer: Send it privately unless you know they like being posted about. Platform-wide, 38.7% of SubhSandesh creators password-protect the page before sharing it (1,961 of 5,061), which suggests private sending is the norm rather than the exception.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Propose Day Wishes: Who Gets One, and When to Send It

Propose Day wishes are greetings you address and send, and on 8 February most go to people you are not proposing to: a partner you already have, a spouse, a friend, a sibling, a work group. A wish is not a proposal, which needs an answer; not a quote, which someone else wrote; and not a shayari, a verse form. This page separates them, gives 15 original wishes sorted by the hour each suits, and says who needs a built page and who needs plain text — against SubhSandesh figures that are platform-wide across 20 page types and none proposal-specific: 5,061 personalised pages built since 12 March 2026, 91.2% of them published and shared (4,615 of 5,061), and 38.7% password-protected before sharing (1,961 of 5,061).

## What a Propose Day wish is, and what it is not

A Propose Day wish is a short addressed greeting sent on Propose Day — 8 February, the second day of Valentine week — to mark the occasion rather than to ask a question. It differs from a proposal in that it expects no answer, from a quote in that it names one person, and from a shayari in that it carries no metrical form.

That decides who may receive it. A proposal has one legitimate recipient and one legitimate outcome; a wish has no such constraint, which is why the day produces messages to spouses, friends, elder sisters and office groups. A quote, being unaddressed, reads as a confession the moment a colleague's name goes on it.

## Propose Day 2027 is Monday 8 February, a working day

Valentine week 2027 opens with Rose Day on Sunday 7 February, runs Propose Day on Monday 8 February and closes with Valentine's Day on Sunday 14 February — eight dated days, Propose Day second.

The weekday matters more than the date. Propose Day 2026 fell on a Sunday; 2027 lands on a working Monday, so last year's free-afternoon plan does not transfer.

Weekday rhythms are measurable. A 2022 open-access analysis of mobile network records in Budapest, [Awakening City](https://doi.org/10.3390/info13030114), found groups become phone-active earlier on workdays than on holidays. A European city, so treat it as evidence that workday and holiday rhythms differ, not a clock for Mumbai.

## 15 Propose Day wishes, grouped by the hour you send them

Every line below was written for this page. Each block gives the window, who it suits, three lines and the risk.

### 1. Before 8 am — landing before the day starts

**The window.** 6 am to 8 am, before the commute.

**Who it suits.** A partner you already have, when you want warmth without obligation.

**Lines.**
- "Happy Propose Day. No question attached — I wanted mine to be the first message on your phone."
- "It's Propose Day and I have nothing to ask you. I got the answer years ago."
- "Before the day swallows you: I would pick you again this morning."

**What it risks.** Little — it expects no reply, and carries nothing heavy.

### 2. Mid-morning, 10 am to noon — the desk wish

**The window.** 10 am to noon, once people are at a desk.

**Who it suits.** Friends, siblings, cousins, family and office groups.

**Lines.**
- "Happy Propose Day to the friend who proofread every message I was too scared to send."
- "Happy Propose Day, everyone. Nobody here is proposing to anybody. Take it as a greeting."
- "Happy Propose Day to my sister, who decided at nine she would vet whoever I married."

**What it risks.** Tone, not timing: a group wish that reads like a confession.

### 3. The lunch hour, 1 pm to 2 pm — expecting a reply

**The window.** 1 pm to 2 pm, the one predictable free block.

**Who it suits.** A partner you will ask something of later, or anyone you want an answer from.

**Lines.**
- "Happy Propose Day. I'm asking you something this evening and I'd rather you weren't ambushed."
- "Happy Propose Day. Free at 8? I have a question and a bad plan for asking it."
- "Happy Propose Day. Not a proposal — a request: name one thing you want this year."

**What it risks.** The only window where a slow reply stings, because you signalled you are waiting.

### 4. Early evening, 6 pm to 8 pm — for a partner of years

**The window.** 6 pm to 8 pm, after work and before dinner.

**Who it suits.** A spouse, or a partner far enough in that the proposal is history.

**Lines.**
- "Happy Propose Day. Years in, the answer is still the least surprising thing about us."
- "Happy Propose Day. You said yes when I had nothing but a plan. Thank you for the risk."
- "Happy Propose Day to the person who already agreed. I'd like to ask again, badly, in the kitchen."

**What it risks.** Preparation, not tone — people build at the last minute and run out of evening.

### 5. After 10 pm — the wish you actually mean

**The window.** After 10 pm, when the phone is the only thing on.

**Who it suits.** One person — the partner you are serious about, or the one you have not told.

**Lines.**
- "Happy Propose Day. I've written this six times. Short version: I want the next thirty years."
- "Happy Propose Day. I'm not asking over text — I'm telling you it's coming, so you can decide how."
- "Happy Propose Day. If you're awake, come to the window. If not, read this and call me."

**What it risks.** Everything the earlier windows do not: late messages are read alone, replies run slower, and a night of silence feels longer than an afternoon.

## Who gets which wish, and which page fits

Five recipients, sorted by what you are sending. Every share is platform-wide across all 20 page types, not a proposal-page figure — no proposal-specific data exists.

| Recipient | What you are sending | Best window | Page, and its share of 5,061 pages since 12 Mar 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Someone you have not asked yet | A proposal, not a wish | After 10 pm, in person | `/proposal` — no proposal-specific figure published |
| A partner of several years | A wish | 6 pm to 8 pm | `/love-gf` — 1,173 pages, 23.2%, the #2 page type |
| A partner you are mid-argument with | An apology first, then a wish | 6 pm to 8 pm | `/apology-dashboard` — 1,347 pages, 26.6%, the #1 page type |
| A friend, sibling or cousin | A greeting | 10 am to noon | None fits — plain text is correct |
| An office or family group | A greeting | 10 am to noon | None fits — a page sent to a group misfires |

Only the top row needs a built page. If you are genuinely asking, the [Will You Marry Me proposal scrapbook](/proposal) is the template: your story page by page, ending in a YES button that grows every time they dodge it.

For rows two and three the honest alternative is the [romantic "I love you" page](/love-gf): those relationships already exist, so the message is affection, not a question. For rows four and five neither template is right, and no template is — a friend or sibling should get plain text in your own words, since a page addressed to them reads either as a joke or as a confession.

One first-party number sets the deadline. The median gap from first save to last edit is 2.4 hours, sampled on `/apology-dashboard` at n=1,348 and not on any proposal page, so an 8 pm page needs a mid-afternoon start. Anything else belongs in the [full template list](/templates).

Two recipients need more than a hub gives: a girlfriend writing to a boyfriend gets the private-versus-public question at [propose-day-wishes-for-boyfriend](/blog/propose-day-wishes-for-boyfriend), and a Hindi wish turns on pronoun choice, with तुम, तू and आप marked per recipient at [propose-day-wishes-in-hindi](/blog/propose-day-wishes-in-hindi).

## What silence after a Propose Day wish does and does not mean

Timing carries meaning by itself: communication research calls this chronemics and treats a delay as a nonverbal cue, not an absence of one.

Lateness is judged against an expectation, not a clock. [Kalman and Rafaeli's 2011 study in *Communication Research*](https://doi.org/10.1177/0093650210378229) tested replies at one day, two weeks and silence beyond a month, and found how a delay was read depended on what the recipient stood to gain. Abstract only; the publisher blocks automated access.

Read receipts sharpen it. A 2020 study of 213 college students in Japan, [Reply Speed as Nonverbal Cue in Text Messaging](https://doi.org/10.4018/ijthi.2020010103), found negative emotions — sadness, anxiety, anger, guilt — arose sooner while waiting for a reply to a message already marked read than to an unread one. On WhatsApp that is blue ticks versus grey; abstract only.

Timing damages trust when it is late *against the recipient's own ideal*, not merely late. A 2026 study of 333 adults in the *Journal of Social and Personal Relationships*, [Too Late to Trust?](https://doi.org/10.1177/02654075261472148), associated later-than-ideal disclosure with lower trust (β = −.27), timing appropriateness accounting for 28.5% of the effect. Abstract only.

The reverse is the useful half. A 2021 open-access experiment on [instructor e-mail response speed](https://aquila.usm.edu/jetde/vol14/iss1/3/) found that replying *faster than expected* was rated more favourably for credibility and relational closeness than replying slowly — the gain comes from beating the expectation, not from raw speed.

## When a Propose Day wish is the wrong thing to send

A wish is the wrong object whenever the day substitutes for a conversation. If you are proposing, a message is a notice, not the proposal — send it, then ask in person.

It is also wrong for anyone who dislikes being marked publicly. Platform-wide, 38.7% of creators password-protect the page before sharing (1,961 of 5,061).

A built page beats plain text only when the recipient opens it. Same room, and speaking wins. No smartphone, and the link is useless — 48.4% of views, platform-wide, are on a phone (27,185 of 56,152).

## Sources

- Kalman & Rafaeli, "Online Pauses and Silence", *Communication Research*, Feb 2011 — [doi:10.1177/0093650210378229](https://doi.org/10.1177/0093650210378229). Abstract only.
- Wang, "Too Late to Trust?", *Journal of Social and Personal Relationships*, 29 July 2026 — [doi:10.1177/02654075261472148](https://doi.org/10.1177/02654075261472148). Abstract only.
- Kato, Kato & Ozawa, "Reply Speed as Nonverbal Cue in Text Messaging", *IJTHI*, 1 Jan 2020 — [doi:10.4018/ijthi.2020010103](https://doi.org/10.4018/ijthi.2020010103). Abstract only.
- Tatum, N., "Student Evaluations of Instructor Email Response Speed as Chronemic Expectancy Violations", *JETDE*, 2021, open access — [aquila.usm.edu/jetde/vol14/iss1/3](https://aquila.usm.edu/jetde/vol14/iss1/3/).
- Pintér & Felde, "Awakening City", *Information*, 26 Feb 2022, open access — [doi:10.3390/info13030114](https://doi.org/10.3390/info13030114). Abstract only.
